summary:
Anambra State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches conduct well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch reported in October 2014 that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Anambra lies outside the twelve northern states that apply Shari'a criminal law, so the federal penalties apply here in full and the death-penalty provisions for male sodomy under state Zina rules do not reach this state. Same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law at entry, carrying up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Shari'a provisions in those twelve states criminalise same-sex acts between men and between women.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; it states that same-sex activity is illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment, that some northern states under Shari'a law can prescribe the death penalty, and that the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

Nigeria's federal framework, which governs Anambra, criminalises same-sex sexual activity with up to 14 years' imprisonment in the southern portion and under northern secular law, and death in the twelve northern states applying Shari'a law. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013 extends criminalisation to attempted same-sex marriages. LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria have no legal protections and face frequent violence. In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Anambra is a Nigerian state in the Southeastern region, Igbo-majority, formed in 1976, with capital Awka. Its southern location places it outside the northern zone where the Shari'a criminal-law states sit, so the federal penalties apply in full and the northern Shari'a provisions do not reach this state.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.
localsOnly:
Residents of Anambra live under the federal SSMPA framework with no state-level Shari'a overlay, so the 10 to 14 year penalties for cohabitation, public displays of same-sex relationships and operating gay organisations apply as written. Nigerian LGBTQ+ residents have no statutory protections against discrimination or violence, and police have used the SSMPA to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

The 2022 court ruling striking down Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act as unconstitutional applies nationwide, including in Anambra, though the remainder of the Act's prohibitions remain enforceable.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing in Nigeria have been enacted remains unresolved in the sources available here.

Enforcement patterns specific to Anambra State, as distinct from the national picture, are not sourced in this inventory; the Lagos and Abuja incidents cited illustrate national police practice rather than Anambra-specific conduct.

The Wikipedia-sourced 2022 court ruling on Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act is reported without the court's name or case citation in the inventory, so the ruling's precise scope and current status are not independently verifiable from these sources.
